content_en:
There are 57 million people worldwide living with dementia today. For the researchers working to help them, the obstacle isn’t a lack of effort — it’s too much data, too few experts to synthesize it and a pace of discovery that can’t keep up with the disease.

The Consortium for Biomedical Research and AI in Neurodegeneration (C-BRAIN), working with NVIDIA, is using AI to change that.

Alzheimer’s disease is one of today’s leading global health challenges, with over 10 million new dementia cases diagnosed each year. Despite a 7x increase in National Institutes of Health funding in the last 15 years — reaching $3.9 billion annually — no treatment has been found to stop, prevent or reverse the disease yet.

The bottlenecks are not enough high impact scientific findings, too much data living in institutional silos and too slow a pace of synthesis to keep up with the research that is published.

C-BRAIN, led by Dr. Randall Bateman and a consortium of 18 member institutions across academic, philanthropic, pharma and research organizations, launched in November 2025 to help scientists make better, faster discoveries by accelerating the research that makes new treatments possible.

“We have a window of opportunity with artificial intelligence to do research fundamentally different than we’ve ever done before, in a way that accelerates discoveries to help patients,” said Bateman, founder and director of C-BRAIN and the Charles F. and Joanne Knight Distinguished Professor of Neurology at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. He described their work as “AI tools built by scientists, for scientists.”

The consortium is building a system that harnesses previously untapped Alzheimer’s research data to support scientists’ work.

## **Speeding Research From Weeks to Hours**

Essential assets in Alzheimer’s research are datasets that have never been publicly accessible to AI tools or human researchers. This includes unpublished findings, negative results and governed proprietary data from member institutions.

“A lot of life sciences data doesn’t make its way into the frontier models,” said Dr. Ade Ojewole, chief technology officer of C-BRAIN. “The consequence of that is we’re leaving a lot of intelligence on the table.”

C-BRAIN refers to this as “dark data,” which slows down Alzheimer’s research.

Some dark data is directly deposited into secure computer systems for AI tools to access. To use this data without compromising patient privacy or institutional governance, C-BRAIN uses a hybrid centralized and federated approach — where AI models learn from data at each institution without that data ever having to leave its walls. This kind of infrastructure is technically demanding to build and scale, which is part of what NVIDIA brings to the collaboration.

C-BRAIN currently runs 64 NVIDIA data center GPUs on premises alongside cloud-based nodes on Microsoft Azure, with additional NVIDIA GPU capacity, including NVIDIA Blackwell systems, on the horizon as the consortium’s ambitions scale.

To explore how AI and accelerated computing can advance Alzheimer’s research while navigating its technical demands, C-BRAIN is working with NVIDIA to incorporate technologies including the NVIDIA BioNeMo open developer platform and the MONAI framework for C-BRAIN’s research pipelines.

“The C-BRAIN collaboration with NVIDIA aims to unlock those models in a way that they can deliver something quite impactful and important,” said Bateman.

“A great deal of optimization is going to be needed as we push the boundaries of what today’s spatial omics machine learning architectures can model,” Ojewole said. “NVIDIA software is definitely going to come into play there.”

Researchers at C-BRAIN have already built two tools: OpenScientist — built with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory in an effort led by research scientist Justin Reese — and InsightEngine, built with 387 Labs.

OpenScientist is an open source agentic AI co-scientist that takes a scientist’s research question and dataset, then semi-autonomously generates hypotheses, runs analyses and produces verifiable, auditable insights. InsightEngine is an open source research platform that uses agentic AI to test hypotheses against the scientific literature, analyzing user-supplied datasets, exploring a biomedical knowledge graph and checking every claim against evidence to catch hallucinations before researchers commit to costly experiments.

In published case studies, OpenScientist completed analyses in minutes that domain scientists estimated would take weeks to months, at a cost of under $10 per run. At C-BRAIN’s current reach of over 200 research groups, this capability could release substantial research capacity, potentially exceeding one million hours annually at scale.

## **From Correlation to Cause**

Looking ahead, C-BRAIN aims to build a multimodal biological foundation model trained on the full breadth of its data — neuroimaging, multi-omics, fluid biomarkers and longitudinal clinical measures.

By year three, it aims to discover new causal mechanisms of brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease, moving to testable scientific principles using the full scope of available research and data.

Bateman said, “AI that can think and reason has the potential to accelerate discoveries that will lead to powerful and implementable preventions and treatments for the entire population.”

title: London-based Machenta, which is building an AI model that can teach robots new physical tasks after seeing them performed just once, raised a $40M seed

title_en: London-based Machenta, which is building an AI model that can teach robots new physical tasks after seeing them performed just once, raised a $40M seed
excerpt_en: London-based Machenta, which is building an AI model that can teach robots new physical tasks after seeing them performed just once, raised a $40M seed
content_en:
A London-based robotics startup is betting it can teach robots new tricks without collecting the mountains of real-world data its much bigger rivals are chasing.

Machenta, founded by researchers from Imperial College London, has raised a $40 million seed round to build an AI model that can teach robots new physical tasks after seeing them performed just once, the company exclusively told Business Insider. Venture capital firms Creandum and Union Square Ventures co-led the round. Machenta declined to disclose its valuation.

While rivals building general-purpose AI models for robots are scrambling to amass real-world data, Machenta is taking a contrarian approach. Edward Johns, the startup's CEO and cofounder, and an Imperial professor, said the company trains its model in computer-generated environments that mimic how objects move and interact, without using a "single pixel of real-world data."

Once trained, the model can direct a robot to perform a new task, such as tidying a table or putting objects into a box, after watching it done just once, without further training, Johns said. In a video shared with Business Insider, three robots pack and close a box on an assembly line, a task Johns said they learned this way.

The startup has 11 employees and remains focused on research, with no near-term plans to commercialize its technology. Its model can learn some tasks immediately, but more precise tasks and complex movements remain challenging.

Machenta faces rivals with multibillion-dollar valuations in one of robotics' most competitive and well-funded fields. Its California-based competitors include Physical Intelligence, valued at roughly $11 billion, and FieldAI, which is raising funding at a $10 billion valuation, Business Insider reported this month.

Another rival, Skild AI, which is valued at over $14 billion, is already selling technology with similar capabilities. In August, Skild unveiled a model that it said could perform previously unseen tasks lasting up to 10 minutes after a single video demonstration. Last month, it said that it had reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue from more than 60 customers.

### **From research lab to startup**

Six years ago, Johns began investigating whether robots could learn new physical tasks as quickly as humans at his Imperial College lab.

In the lab's early experiments, researchers physically guided a robot through a task, such as picking up a spatula and scooping an object. The robot then spent about 30 minutes collecting additional data about the object and its surroundings before it could perform the task on its own.

Johns and former Ph.D. student Vitalis Vosylius spent the next few years working to eliminate that extra step, founding Machenta late last year after seeing early signs that their model could perform new tasks immediately after a demonstration.

Companies are increasingly buying and collecting data to teach robots how to interact with the real world. But Johns believes simply collecting more data isn't the answer. It also remains unclear how much training data will be needed to make general-purpose robots a reality. Johns said that Machenta is taking on the harder challenge of designing algorithms that can generate synthetic data useful for teaching robots physical tasks.

Machenta plans to use the funding to expand its team and train its model with more computing power and simulated data, hoping to teach robots to perform more precise and complex tasks.

### Regal debuts Goal Oriented Agents, putting an actor and a director model on every call

Enterprise voice artificial intelligence company Regal Voice Inc. today added Goal Oriented Agents to its platform, enabling businesses using them to define what a call has to accomplish, and providing two AI models that split the work of getting there.

The new agents are aimed at a problem Regal says shows up in calls such as auto insurance claims, in which someone reporting an accident tends to explain what happened, where and who was involved in one go. Agents built on conditional logic often circle back for details the caller already gave, just so each field gets filled. Building the whole agent on a single prompt keeps the conversation open, and in Regal’s view it leaves business processes only loosely followed.

Goal Oriented Agents put two models on each call. Regal calls them an actor and a director, and both start work as soon as the caller stops talking. The actor, a smaller and faster model tuned for dialogue, replies right away. Running behind it, the director checks whether the goals for the current stage have been met and can move the call to a new stage with fresh instructions for the actor.

Businesses build the agents out of goal nodes, each listing the goals to be met by the end of the node and any prerequisites that come first. Booking a callback can count as one of those goals. A prerequisite is something the agent has to establish before it can act, such as the caller’s date of birth. Regal said those can be written as plain-language conditions too, for example “the caller mentioned a death in the family.”

The director reviews progress after every turn, so one answer can tick off several items at once. Regal’s sample auto insurance claim has a caller named Dan describing the vehicle damage, photo evidence and injuries in his first message. All three get marked as collected, and the agent goes straight to his name. Once it has that, the director sees location and policy number are still missing, so the actor’s next question is where he is.

Regal said complex intake and qualification calls are among the strongest uses it has seen for the agents. The company named Medicare enrollment, roadside assistance and mortgage qualification as uses the design opens up. Medical intake that complies with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act is another.

Google LLC, AAA and Toyota Motor Corp. are among the more than 200 enterprises Regal says it serves. Customers of Five9 Inc.’s contact center platform gained access to Regal’s voice agents through an integration in August.

Regal is a venture capital-backed startup that has raised $83 million to date. That includes a $40 million round in October 2024.

# Google Deepmind's Genie 4 puts a modern spin on agent designs that predate LLMs

## Key Points

- Google Deepmind has introduced Genie 4, an interactive world model that calculates environments frame by frame in real time and, for the first time, directly generates matching background audio and character dialogue.
- Gemini models steer events in the background, planning multistep tasks and continuously adapting the simulated world to user text prompts and changing conditions.
- Genie 4 is still an experimental research model with limitations in longer sessions and complex physics. Access is limited to select testers for now and will later expand to Google AI Ultra subscribers.

**Genie 4 is supposed to simulate interactive worlds in real time, including sound and talking characters. Gemini models plan in the background what happens next in the simulation. Only select testers can try the world model for now.**

Google Deepmind has introduced Genie 4, the successor to Genie 3, which the company showed in August 2025. The world model doesn't produce finished videos but calculates a scene frame by frame, reacting to input as it goes. Users move through the scene with the keyboard and steer events with text prompts.

According to Deepmind, Genie 4 is the company's first real-time world model that generates sound directly. The company says each world has its own background audio, such as wind in the trees. Genie 4 also handles dialogue, with characters that are supposed to talk to each other and react in real time to user input or events.

Deepmind sees the biggest gain in realism in how the model renders people. Characters are supposed to move naturally and react to their surroundings, and users should be able to control them directly.

## Gemini models plan ahead to keep the world coherent

According to Deepmind, Genie 4 builds on capabilities of the video model Gemini Omni so the world looks and behaves realistically. Other Gemini models help plan the simulation to keep it consistent.

If a user changes the weather with a text prompt, Gemini is supposed to adapt the instruction to the running scene. Deepmind says Gemini also steers events between inputs so the world keeps developing in a way that makes sense.

Deepmind explains the process with multistep tasks. Gemini 3.8 Flash watches the scene continuously, breaks a goal into steps, and uses new frames to check whether each step worked. If the world changes or the user steps in, the model adjusts its plan.

Deepmind is also testing Gemini 4 Argon to tie its Genie work to its robotics research, Gemini Robotics. In one demo, Argon breaks the task of playing checkers into steps. Genie 4 gets these as text instructions and uses them to simulate Apptronik's humanoid robot Apollo playing the game, with no real robot involved.

## Longer sessions still trip up the model

Deepmind calls Genie 4 an early, experimental model. According to the company, the world stays consistent over short sessions, but visual details can shift and objects don't always persist in longer simulations or after several complex prompt changes.

Deepmind says it's still researching complex physical interactions, accurate real-time sound, and readable text.

For now, Genie 4 is only available to select testers as a research preview. It's set to reach Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Project Genie web app soon, along with partners who have early access to the Gemini API and Google AI Studio.

Google says all videos and audio tracks will carry its SynthID watermark, which invisibly marks AI-generated content.

Once they mature, world models could serve as training environments where robots and AI agents learn from simulated experience rather than just from data. Deepmind sees pairing Gemini with Genie as an early step toward hybrid world models that combine the reasoning of language and code models with pixel-level simulation.

title: Google’s Genie 4 world model adds audio, more realistic worlds, and real-time steering
excerpt: Google DeepMind released Genie 4, a world model with real-time audio, more realistic simulations, and mid-simulation text prompts, in research preview for trusted testers.
title_en: Google’s Genie 4 world model adds audio, more realistic worlds, and real-time steering
excerpt_en: Google DeepMind released Genie 4, a world model with real-time audio, more realistic simulations, and mid-simulation text prompts, in research preview for trusted testers.
content_en:
Google DeepMind released its newest world model, Genie 4, in research preview on Tuesday. The latest model generates the most photorealistic and interactive worlds yet, allowing users to type prompts mid-simulation to change the scene. The model also generates real-time audio that matches the simulated world, including music, ambient noises, and interactive dialogue.

The release of Genie 4 comes a couple of months after AI video startup Runway released its second world model, GWM Worlds 2, a playable model that responds dynamically to user inputs and includes audio generation. At the same time, the world model industry is beginning to consolidate. Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs is being acquired by AMD, Amazon is in talks to buy Decart, and Rivian just acquired Third Dimension to bring simulation capabilities in-house for self-driving testing.

Genie 4 is Google’s latest move to stay ahead in the crowded field.

Google released its predecessor, Genie 3, as a research preview a little over a year ago. Aside from being far more photorealistic and featuring audio, Genie 4 allows for freeform edits, like changing the weather or camera angle in real time or adding new people or objects. It can maintain a consistent scene for up to two minutes, double its predecessor’s limit, and offers better physics and more human-like characters.

Gemini, Google’s AI model, is also more closely integrated with Genie 4, acting as the director that plans steps and checks frames while Genie creates the visuals. In a research experiment tied to Gemini Robotics, a Gemini 4 Argon model broke down tasks into steps that Genie 4 simulated in real time. The experiment shows a possible way to test robot scenarios in simulation before they happen in the real world.

“What we’ll increasingly see in the future are these hybrid world models, where you have a combination of Gemini writing code and text, and Genie ingesting that in real time and simulating reality at different levels of abstraction,” Tejas Kulkarni, research director at Google, said during a briefing.

As with other world models, the pitched commercial use cases include gaming, interactive learning, and robotics. One speculative example of interactive learning would be entering a painting of a historical scene and chatting to the painting’s subjects about the event portrayed.

But “trusted testers” — the people who get first access to Google cutting-edge products — are pointing to a possible new use: prototyping films.

“The real time aspect becomes most valuable in the areas where keeping a state of flow in the creativity space becomes incredibly useful,” Diego Rivas, a Google DeepMind engineer, said during a press briefing. “For example, in the ideation phase, in the storyboarding phase — anytime you’re kind of in need of rapid ideation.”

Google also offers Veo, its AI video generation model that makes high-definition clips with built-in synchronized audio from text, image, or video prompts — a tool that has been growing in popularity among filmmakers.

Rivas added that users could, eventually, rely on Gemini Omni, a multimodal large language model that can generate video from images, audio, and text, to turn those prototypes into creative assets. Though those capabilities, he says, are still a ways off.

Throughout the briefing, Rivas stressed that it’s still early days for Genie 4, and that it’s not yet clear what the end-to-end product experience will be. The team also acknowledged that Genie 4 still has gaps: details and objects can drift the longer a simulation runs, and they still haven’t quite figured out how to ensure the audio will be accurate and any in-world text will be legible.

Genie 4 is available now as a research preview for trusted testers. In the coming weeks, the model will roll out to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie, Google’s AI tool for generating interactive worlds from text or image prompts, and early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio.

title: UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tech
excerpt: A government watchdog is considering a probe into the Home Office’s use of ChatGPT technology to process asylum claims amid concerns over the tools’ accuracy and secrecy surrounding their use.
title_en: UK Home Office May Face Investigation Over Use of OpenAI Tech
excerpt_en: A government watchdog is considering a probe into the Home Office’s use of ChatGPT technology to process asylum claims amid concerns over the tools’ accuracy and secrecy surrounding their use.
content_en:
A UK government watchdog is considering an investigation into the Home Office’s use of generative AI tools to process asylum applications, WIRED has learned. The potential probe follows lawmakers and researchers publicly questioning the tools’ accuracy and the government’s secrecy around their use.

The Independent Chief Inspector of Borders and Immigration (ICIBI), which monitors the Home Office’s management of borders, immigration, and customs, has asked digital rights nonprofit Open Rights Group (ORG) to share more information on the tools as it draws up plans for the topics it will inspect next year, campaigner Sara Alsherif tells WIRED. ORG’s findings come from a six-month investigation into the tools, which involved 11 parliamentary questions, two ministerial letters, and 10 public records requests that attempt to pry details from the Home Office, which has withheld details on the tools.

The ICIBI tells WIRED it cannot confirm what topics are under active consideration before it publishes its annual inspection priorities, but it says it is aware of concerns about the use of AI tools and pointed to its findings last year that one of the tool’s “effectiveness and reliability were varied.”

“Asylum decisions are made by trained caseworkers, with AI tools used only to assist in navigating interview records and policy information. They cannot be used in isolation and do not make decisions on claims,” a Home Office spokesperson tells WIRED in an email. “We regularly monitor the performance of these tools alongside our established quality-assurance processes, and have already committed to publishing updated evaluations on their roll out.”

The Home Office uses the Asylum Case Summarisation (ACS) and Asylum Policy Search (APS) tools, built on OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 large language model and Microsoft Foundry, to summarize transcripts of interviews with asylum applicants and information about their countries of origin, according to documents obtained by ORG. The immigration and law enforcement authority started piloting these tools in late 2024 as the Labour government tried to clear a backlog of around 100,000 asylum cases, while staying on top of the tens of thousands of new applications the UK receives each year. While the department has made significant progress, halving the number of people waiting on an initial decision in the year through June, the number of appeals against decisions has ballooned.

Researchers are concerned about the accuracy of the AI tools–especially to decide something as high-stakes as whether to send someone back to a country where they fear persecution. ORG found that the percentage of summaries generated by the ACS deemed not fit for use—often because they contain factual errors or misrepresentations—is significantly higher than the published 9 percent error rate calculated in the pilot evaluation. There is no quality control for the summaries produced by the APS, it also found.

Asylum decision-makers use the tools to save time when reviewing asylum cases; when used together, the pilot showed the tools could save around an hour per case, according to government estimates. Caseworkers use the ACS to speed up their review of transcripts of interviews where asylum seekers explain how they were persecuted in their country and why they are afraid to return. They use the APS as a search assistant to find and summarize country policy information, which informs them whether the applicant faces a genuine risk of harm in their home country. In July, a UK judge accused the Home Office of citing an “AI hallucinated” document to refuse a Moroccan woman and her child’s asylum claim on the basis that her home country would be safe for her to return to.

“We’re dealing with people’s lives. We’re talking about people that have faced some of the worst circumstances, and we’re meant to be making decisions based on facts and on understanding harm,” Labour backbench MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy tells WIRED. “I just don’t think it’s appropriate that machines are doing that.”

A Home Office spokesperson says, “Use of Artificial Intelligence is just one of the tools at our disposal to protect our borders, and does not replace or automate the role of human decision-makers.”

Ribeiro-Addy, Alsherif, and the Public Law Project, which has separately been investigating the tools, also worry that well-documented “cultural bias” in GPT models could lead to language barriers and the loss of cultural nuances in the summaries, which could in turn result in discriminatory decisions. An OpenAI spokesperson highlighted to WIRED the company’s ongoing work to improve its models’ accuracy and pointed out that the company will be retiring GPT-4 in January.

In the absence of regulation, the UK’s “AI Playbook” mandates that departments must be transparent about the algorithmic tools they use in decision-making processes and make information on them available to the public, including listing those tools on a public repository. The Home Office’s case summarization and policy search tools are not on that list.

Asylum seekers are also not told when these AI tools are used in their case. “Migrant organizations, legal practitioners, not many of them know about the actual use of this tool,” says Alsherif, who leads ORG’s migrant digital justice program. “So we need to let them know about this, let them know how it works, so they can challenge it.” Not being able to contest an incorrect AI summary of their personal information may breach UK data rights laws, Cloisters lawyers wrote in an independent legal opinion commissioned by ORG. The Home Office states that parts of the decision-making process may involve automation in its privacy notice.

Both groups have sent their findings to UK data regulator, the Information Commission, which is currently investigating the Home Office’s refusal to tell ORG how staff use and were trained to use two AI tools.

Public Law Project senior research fellow Caroline Selman also notes that the ACS and APS tools are just two of the 11 high-risk AI systems that her team has found being used across government but absent from the public repository. She’s concerned there may be more deployed across government that even researchers, let alone the individuals they are being used on, are unaware of.

“Other tools are being used but not being publicized at all,” says Selman, “and you can’t even begin to ask questions about things if you don’t know that they’re being used.”

title: Meta AI director Rohit Patel leaves to take on Microsoft Office and Google Workspace
excerpt: Rohit Patel is departing Meta after eight years working on AI evaluations and reinforcement learning, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. His startup, Ndoc, aims to take on Microsoft Office Suite.
title_en: Meta AI director Rohit Patel leaves to take on Microsoft Office and Google Workspace
excerpt_en: Rohit Patel is departing Meta after eight years working on AI evaluations and reinforcement learning, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. His startup, Ndoc, aims to take on Microsoft Office Suite.
content_en:
After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs has launched Ndoc, a startup he’s pitching as an AI-native replacement for Microsoft Office suite or Google Workspace.

Patel is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures from Meta following the exits of Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan, AI researcher Andrew Tulloch, and Head of Product for AI-for-Work Emily Dalton Smith.

Patel designed Ndoc to be more than just another AI tool layered onto an existing workflow. The goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit, and “ChatGPT copy-paste” with one unified workspace that all colleagues can access, even if they’re not signed up for Ndoc.

Ndoc brings three components together in one layout. The Stage tab is where presentations of key findings live, like slide decks, dashboards, simulations, or mini apps. The Narrative tab features analyses, numbered citations, generated figures, and generally the “why” behind the numbers. The Model tab is where underlying datasets and Python scripts are housed.

The design reflects Patel’s background. During his tenure at Meta, Patel focused on reinforcement learning — a type of machine learning in which AI agents learn to make decisions through trial and error and maximize rewards — and evaluating whether AI output is trustworthy. Patel believes that if AI is going to build the spreadsheets and slide decks that companies use to make decisions, someone should be able to check its work. For instance, users can find the Python scripts used to create the documents.

“Even if you don’t know any Python, you can ask \[the AI chat\] to explain, ‘Hey, what does this script do? Which line has my formula?’ And you can verify that formula,” Patel said. “There’s nothing hidden behind the curtain here.”

In practice, users can upload a dataset and ask Ndoc to perform an analysis and write a narrative about the findings. They can also add document-specific context, including audience, tone, and memory. “It maintains a memory across your person, that particular document, your team, and your company,” Patel said.

Patel also says Ndoc is built and fine-tuned using a mixture of open source models. Because the platform was developed from scratch, he says it costs considerably less to run than alternatives built on frontier AI models.

“I thought that’s what people would be excited about, but people don’t care about that,” he said, referring to his early trial users. “What people are excited about is that they love seeing all their end-to-end in one place.”

Patel’s larger ambition is to reinvent the file itself. He says documents can be exported as a single “.ndoc.html” file that can be opened in any browser, a format he plans to open-source so other developers can build apps that work with it without being locked into Ndoc the way so many have been locked into Microsoft or Google for years.

His desire to open-source this project was partly why he left Meta and decided to go it alone. At a big company like Meta, getting everyone to agree on an open source format would undoubtedly require the input of “hundreds of people and opinions on how the format should look.”

Patel wanted to move quickly. “Humans can only move at human pace, whereas…I can move at the pace of what AI can do.”

Trying to become the platform where enterprise work happens is a huge bet for a founder with a team of three and no funding, especially when other AI labs are trying to own the same space.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, SpaceXAI, and Google have all come out with enterprise AI tools that allow users to connect to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other workplace apps so their AI models can work directly in those tools. And last month, OpenAI launched Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT that’s a more direct competitor to those established tools.

Patel acknowledges that Space could be a threat, but says the labs largely have the wrong idea.

“Companies are basically attaching AI to spreadsheets and it fills your cells for you,” he said. “It just sort of kills my soul. This is like if you just figured out electricity, and then you decided the best use case is to put lights on my bulls that till my soil. No. Get a tractor.”

There’s a reason the AI labs have tried to bring their models to where people are already working, though. It’s hard to change habits and replace entire workflows. Patel says he understands that, which is why he built connectors so customers can import existing data from the tools they already use.

“My bar was that I’m not going to release anything I don’t love using,” he said. “I have very optimized AI workflows for everything I do. If I start using this tool, and I keep going back to my workflows, I haven’t built a good enough tool…I have a graveyard of tools that did not meet that bar.”

Patel has a similar bar for gaining customer traction before he tries to raise funds. “I didn’t want to take money until I had some proof that people love the product,” he said.

As of Tuesday, Ndoc is conducting an enterprise pilot and opening an alpha version to a limited number of customers who join the wait list. It’s free to sign up, but customers will pay for usage and tokens. He hopes to release a beta version in the coming weeks, with a full launch planned for next year.

For Patel, moving as fast as possible is more important than having the perfect product from the get-go.

“Execution is extremely cheap…so go execute on a suboptimal plan and worry about it later,” he said. “By the time you make the best plan, the execution will be done by somebody else.”

content_en:
# Former Deepmind researcher thinks AlphaGo's playbook can cure AI hallucinations

## Key Points

- Former Deepmind researcher Thore Graepel founded Metis Reasoning to make AI systems more reliable and verifiable, using AlphaGo's approach as a blueprint.
- The method separates knowledge from model weights and stores it in an external ledger, where an independent module checks every assumption against evidence.
- The approach aims to cut hallucinations and provide source-backed explanations, but so far it exists only as a theoretical framework with no working system.

**Former Deepmind researcher Thore Graepel wants to build AI systems that track what they know and check every conclusion against evidence. Larger language models won't fix this problem, his team says.**

Thore Graepel believes the same idea that let AlphaGo beat Go professional Lee Sedol in 2016 can make AI systems more reliable, including in robots. The former Deepmind researcher founded Metis Reasoning and laid out the approach at Nvidia's GTC conference in Berlin, where the chipmaker has been expanding its platform for robotics and physical AI with the goal of turning robotics' data problem into a compute problem.

## A knowledge ledger instead of knowledge baked into model weights

Today's language models amount to just AlphaGo's prediction network, which suggested possible moves, according to Metis. AlphaGo paired that network with a systematic search through game sequences and found the famous Move 37, a move the network would have given a human player roughly a one-in-ten-thousand chance of making. Metis wants to bring that kind of search to general reasoning.

Doing so requires what the company's paper calls an explicit knowledge ledger, comparable to the game board. Similar ideas already exist: Microsoft's GraphRAG organizes knowledge outside model weights in a knowledge graph, and Google's AlphaGeometry2 pairs a language model with a symbolic engine that verifies mathematical proofs. Metis wants to extend those principles to open questions in the real world.

Its knowledge ledger records what is known, how confident the system is, and which questions remain open. A separate module checks new entries against calculations, formal proofs, or empirical evidence, and when an assumption falls away, every conclusion that depended on it gets re-evaluated. A "move" can be a question, an experiment, or a challenge to an existing assumption; the system picks whichever one reduces uncertainty about the original question the most, ultimately delivering either an answer or a justified abstention.

As in AlphaGo, two neural networks suggest and evaluate moves, trained on logged prior investigations but unable to override the verification rules. Metis says the setup should produce fewer hallucinations, explanations with source citations, and knowledge that can be changed or deleted without retraining. Because reasoning breaks into small steps, the approach could also favor smaller models running on edge devices and in robots.

## Companies still don't trust language models enough to deploy them

More data and compute improve language models but don't solve the technology's fundamental problems, according to Metis: the models fabricate answers, their reasoning chains can't be verified, and their knowledge is locked inside the weights. Hallucinations come from the training process itself, the paper argues, because models learn to produce plausible text rather than true text, and even the chains of thought in today's reasoning models often fail to show how an answer was actually reached.

That, the paper says, is why AI has had so little economic impact so far. When an agent acts on behalf of a company, errors are hard to trace back to their source and wrong knowledge can't be removed from the model. AI took off in software engineering because code is easy to test and roll back, but in medicine, finance, chip design, and robotics, the paper argues, AI needs to be verifiable from the ground up.

The white paper describes only a research program, with no working system, no benchmarks, and no comparisons with current reasoning models. The team acknowledges that the real world, unlike Go, provides only partial information, that evidence can be expensive to obtain, and that some questions simply have no answer. The biggest open question is how a verified knowledge ledger would take shape in messy domains beyond textbook examples, given that symbolic AI systems once failed precisely because all their knowledge had to be entered by hand.

## After Silver and Rocktäschel, another Deepmind veteran strikes out on his own

Graepel earned his PhD in machine learning in Berlin in 2001, according to his website. At Microsoft Research he helped build TrueSkill, the matchmaking system behind Xbox Live. He then moved to Deepmind, where he worked on AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero. After a stint at Altos Labs he most recently served on Google Deepmind's post-AGI team, which he left over the summer. He also holds the machine learning chair at University College London. According to Bloomberg, Graepel is raising a low tens-of-millions round for Metis, with a follow-on of several hundred million dollars at a higher valuation already in the works.

He's the latest architect of Deepmind's best-known breakthroughs to build something outside Google. Former colleague David Silver founded Ineffable Intelligence and closed the largest seed round of any European startup. Tim Rocktäschel co-founded Recursive, now valued at $4.65 billion. Others are going straight to competitors. According to the Financial Times, Deepmind dissolved the team behind AlphaFold, and Nobel laureate John Jumper left for Anthropic with two colleagues. CNBC traces the talent drain partly to limited internal access to Google's TPU chips and bureaucracy, while Deepmind itself is losing its independence and founder Demis Hassabis has stepped back from day-to-day operations.

### Edge Sound raises $2M to help physical AI make sense of audio

Edge Sound Research Inc. today announced it has raised $2 million in new funding to build audio infrastructure that isolates useful sounds and combines them with other sensor data to help physical AI systems understand what’s happening in real time.

Stormbreaker Ventures led the round, bringing the company’s total funding to $9 million.

When the company first approached this problem, it looked at sports. When a basketball hits the court, fans are stomping in the stands and bass pounds through the arena’s speakers – all of this comes through microphones at the same time. For an artificial intelligence system trying to isolate the dribble, those overlapping sounds can make this difficult.

This challenge sits at the center of Edge Sound Research’s approach to machine perception: connecting audio with tracking and visual data to determine which sound belongs to which object.

“The issue in audio is it’s not object oriented; it’s channel oriented,” co-founder and Chief Executive Valtteri Salomaki told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

For broadcasters, making that connection means following a player’s sounds through a crowded arena. Edge is betting the same approach could help robots and other physical AI systems interpret the world around them — including activity their cameras cannot yet see.

Humans do this automatically because we exist in a multimodal world: Sight, sound and physical sensation all come in at once. In the physical AI world, sound has always been treated as a second-class citizen to vision because cameras are already everywhere, in everyday life and used for everything. For humans, sound is fundamental to navigating everywhere.

Audio comes in channels, Salomaki explained. It’s connected to microphones, which are positioned around a space or on objects and they listen in locations. These produce signals that identify sounds – they don’t directly associate with anything until something else turns them into readily identifiable information.

“It’s split into two layers,” Salomaki said. “One is how do you create a digital twin of all sensors. The other one is how do you create AI machine learning models to source separate sound elements.”

In the sports arena demonstration, the system uses microphone locations, pickup patterns and player tracking to select useful audio. It then associates locations; visual and audio are paired to identify objects — such as players, the ball, even the coach or a referee with the whistle.

The company said users can import 3D spaces or 2D layouts with coordinates and place sensors within that representation. This allows a spatial map of the environment and its sensors; this is essentially the “digital twin” that Salomaki is referring to.

Other use cases could involve autonomous vehicles, which could be given digital ears to hear if a siren is approaching. Humans identify sounds and direction because our ears are on the sides of our heads. If a sound comes from the left, it’s louder on that side, even if we can’t see an object there.

Anyone who has heard a siren approaching or receding has also experienced the Doppler effect, where the pitch increases or decreases depending on how fast it’s coming or going. A higher pitch can give an autonomous vehicle an immediate warning that an emergency vehicle is approaching from a blind corner (and its direction of approach), even if the lights aren’t visible on camera.

**Building the models for audio perception**

Edge has a general model that it develops and fine-tunes for customer needs. These models face different delay target requirements for real-time activity. Salomaki cited a sub-33-millisecond tolerance for sports broadcasting and said other environments might tolerate 100 or 200 milliseconds.

Useful perception needs to arrive on time for most applications because hearing what happens needs to be paired with seeing.

The company is building toward hardware independence with its digital twin software and AI models, allowing Edge to assemble new applications around a core technology. This way, it will become audio infrastructure that will work alongside existing microphones and cameras customers already have for their current physical AI robots, media and other systems.

With the funding, Salomaki said, Edge will complete integration with existing enterprise customers and make the platform’s components transferable across industries ahead of a Series A.

Live sports has already given Edge a commercial market as it developed and validated its perception technology, using that to help train and build its models. Its Virtual Sound Engine, which automatically captures and isolates sound from complex environments, is already deployed commercially across the industry. Customers and partners include American audio equipment manufacturer Shure Inc., the National Basketball Association, Fox Sports Media Group and the United States Tennis Association Inc.

“In order to achieve the result everybody wants in physical AI, computers need to become a little bit more human,” Salomaki said.

title_en: General Compute raises $100 million Series A, countering the neocloud disaster narrative
excerpt_en: General Compute is betting on inference chips from outside the Nvidia ecosystem.
content_en:
CoreWeave, a publicly traded neocloud that rents out computing power for AI, has seen its stock price fall to a 12-month low, and Elon Musk is flexing $40 billion in debt for buying computing capacity and predicting that “200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation.” It’s not exactly the ideal week to announce a Series A for a neocloud.

General Compute co-founder and CEO Finn Puklowski is unfazed. He’s bullish on CoreWeave’s chances, and thinks Musk is just talking his book to drive down the prices of the GPUs he wants to buy. Fears of a chip-led collapse are “massively overstated. I have people calling me up every single week asking me to do TPUs, GPUs, any chip, to get them more compute.”

Just as important, he says, Anthropic’s bullish S-1 is “settling fears for today.”

General Compute has found a niche building its cloud out of specialized inference chips built by Nvidia rivals. The company struck a $400 million deal to purchase new chips from SambaNova — the first debt financing of inference chips — and now has added Positron and Cerebras to its portfolio of chip suppliers.

A deal with a large customer worth $100 million in annual recurring revenue has paved the way for the company to raise $100 million in Series A funding led by Blackbird Ventures and Abstract Ventures. Valued at $60 million after a May seed round, General Compute is now worth $800 million post-money to its investors.

The startup’s strategy is to zig where others zag. It focused on chips built for inference while everyone else chased GPUs. And instead of taking on a complex effort to build huge data centers, it uses smaller power sources, rents space in other companies’ data centers, and converts former bitcoin-mining sites into places that run AI models.

That approach means General Compute isn’t going to catapult into the top ranks of neoclouds or compete with hyperscalers any time soon. But it’s also not subject to the constraints that come with building data centers from scratch. When General Compute has chips, it will have someplace to plug them in. Puklowski expects the company to deploy 75 megawatts of computing capacity in 2027, and he suspects he will have access to 200 megawatts of power—“more than we can probably fund and get hardware for.”

Still, the plan has a limit. Puklowski’s financing work isn’t done—”capital is going to be a full-time job for me, both on debt and equity,” he told TechCrunch.

The startup has found key customers in cloud companies that specialize in offering developers high-speed inference; General Compute provides the bare metal, or raw servers with no software layered on top, for them to bring their offerings to market. James Palmer, a principal at Blackbird who co-led the round, said his firm’s confidence in General Compute comes in part from an investment in Baseten, an inference cloud company.

“We’ve been proximate to their journey over the last 10 months and observing the wild growth story that \[Baseten\] has gone on, and the demand for open weight inference, and for companies owning their own intelligence,” Palmer told TechCrunch. When it comes to General Compute, he said, “Cerebras, Positron, SambaNova, all need distribution partners who can take them to scale, who can navigate the complexity of the physical world.”

Executives at all three chipmakers sang General Compute’s praises to TechCrunch, each noting the importance of the company’s focus on making the economics of AI cloud compute work. “Everyone in this market is selling speed,” Rodrigo Liang, SambaNova’s CEO and co-founder, said. “The real question is whether you can make money doing it.”

# OpenAI asks outside experts, including a Nobel laureate, to check proofs its AI produced in math, computer science, and physics

**OpenAI says its internal models have disproved a central assumption in computer science and proved part of one of the Millennium Prize Problems, among other results. Outside experts will now decide whether the proofs hold up.**

OpenAI laid out three results from math, computer science, and physics in a blog post. The company says its internal AI models produced the proofs. OpenAI calls the manuscripts a kind of raw research data that still needs to be understood.

So OpenAI asked outside experts to act as "shepherds" for the results. Based on their advice, the company is handling each field differently. OpenAI says it also translated the math and computer science proofs into Lean.

Lean is a programming language that lets a computer check every step of a proof. That doesn't guarantee the result is error-free, though. Lean only checks whether the proof establishes the statement as it was written in Lean. Experts still have to decide whether that statement actually captures the intended problem.

## If OpenAI is right, a core assumption in computer science is wrong

The computer science result centers on the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH). It concerns the Boolean satisfiability problem, or SAT. SAT deals with a logical formula whose variables can only be true or false. The question is whether you can set the variables so the whole formula comes out true.

With only a few variables, you can just try every combination. But each new variable doubles the number of possibilities. With 100 variables, you're already looking at a 31-digit number.

Put simply, the ETH says there's no real shortcut. You can speed up the trial and error, but in the worst case, computing time still grows exponentially, increasing by a fixed factor with every added variable.

OpenAI says the satisfiability problem is closely tied to the P versus NP problem. That's the famous open question of whether a problem whose solution can be checked quickly can also be solved quickly. With SAT, checking is easy because you just plug in a proposed answer and do the math. The hard part is finding one that works.

SAT is considered the textbook example of hard problems of this kind. A fast method for solving it would instantly make thousands of other problems fast to solve too. Most experts believe no such method exists. That belief goes by the shorthand "P does not equal NP."

The ETH goes further than that conjecture. It says not only that SAT is hard, but how hard. If the ETH falls, P could still differ from NP, so hard problems wouldn't automatically become easy.

The ETH was widely accepted as true. Hundreds of papers in graph theory, computational biology, databases, and computational geometry build on it. They show, for example, that a problem can't be solved faster than a certain time if the ETH holds.

Now OpenAI says its system has proved the ETH is false. If the proof holds, those papers lose their foundation. Their results wouldn't automatically be wrong, but they'd no longer be proven.

OpenAI says the result could help researchers find better algorithms. Turning it into practical gains would still take a lot of research, though.

## The practical payoff is unclear, but the theoretical fallout would be big

SAT matters a lot in practice. Specialized programs called SAT solvers check chip designs for errors and test software, for example.

They often handle formulas with millions of variables already. That's because formulas from real-world applications are usually much easier than the worst case the ETH deals with. Speeding up only the worst case wouldn't automatically help these programs.

MIT professor Ryan Williams struck a similarly cautious tone on X. When a user asked what everyday developers would notice first, Williams said nobody knows yet. At the current pace, he said, it's plausible that practical SAT solving could see serious progress within 12 months. "Or we may see nothing of the sort. I really don't know," he admitted.

The result would also ripple through complexity theory itself, specifically the study of circuits, which are networks of simple logic gates like AND, OR, and NOT. If OpenAI's result holds, Williams says it would follow that a certain class of very demanding problems can't be solved with small circuits. "Small" here means that when the input doubles in length, the circuit needs at most about twice as many gates.

## The people who came up with the ETH are checking whether it's wrong

Williams will independently check and explain the result together with Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi of UC San Diego. Impagliazzo and Paturi originally proposed the ETH along with Francis Zane. Williams writes that the group hasn't signed any nondisclosure agreements, is working unpaid, and plans to share interim findings as they go.

In an open letter, the three also make clear that their involvement isn't an endorsement of the claim. A result this big needs careful, independent review, they write.

At the group's request, OpenAI is publishing all the raw data, including the written proof and the Lean proof. The company has also committed to funding a conference on what the result means for the field.

## A decades-old wave conjecture may now hold in every dimension

The math result concerns a conjecture about waves like those in sound, light, or earthquakes. Mathematician Christopher Sogge proposed it in 1991.

Waves can concentrate at a single spot, much like light at the focal point of a magnifying glass. The conjecture says this extreme concentration only lasts briefly. Averaged over time, waves behave more smoothly, or evenly, than the extreme case would suggest. That's why it's called the local smoothing conjecture.

Until now, it had only been proven in two dimensions, for waves on a surface like water. Guth, Wang, and Zhang did that in 2019. OpenAI says its models have now produced a proof for every dimension, including waves in space and in hypothetical spaces with even more dimensions.

OpenAI says the result reaches beyond waves. Because the local smoothing conjecture is so basic to the field, two other well-known conjectures follow from it. They are the Kakeya conjecture from geometry and Stein's restriction conjecture from Fourier analysis. Fourier analysis breaks signals like sounds into individual oscillations. Proving the local smoothing conjecture automatically proves both of these as well.

The Kakeya conjecture shows how hard even these follow-on results are. Wang and Zahl only proved it for three dimensions in 2025. According to OpenAI, both conjectures would now be solved in all dimensions.

Unlike the other two results, no dedicated group is shepherding this proof. OpenAI says it did reach out to an outside expert to discuss that kind of collaboration. On that person's advice, though, the company published the proof text and the Lean proof directly. That way, researchers can decide for themselves how to check the result.

## OpenAI wants to put quantum field theory on solid mathematical ground

The physics result goes to the foundation of particle physics. Physicists describe elementary particles and the forces between them using quantum field theory, which OpenAI calls the most important framework in modern theoretical physics. Its predictions are extremely accurate, but the theories lack an exact mathematical basis.

Instead, physicists work with approximations, such as an imaginary lattice of points that they keep making finer. It's still an open question whether this produces a unique, consistent theory, meaning whether a theory "exists" in the mathematical sense. Whether it describes nature correctly is a separate question.

content_en:
In Marvel’s *VisionQuest*, a superpowered robot tries to better understand humanity by getting lost in elaborate, digital daydreams in which he and other artificial intelligence-powered beings live together in a home. The series is deeply fantastical, yet it plays with some of the ideas that have come to dominate the conversation about real-world generative artificial intelligence, exploring whether we should look at thinking machines as people and if AI truly poses the kind of existential danger that should keep us up at night. It’s also a reminder how aggressively Silicon Valley has used the trappings of science fiction to sell us on its AI products.

# VisionQuest is what happens when AI really goes rogue

Marvel’s latest Disney Plus series is a reminder of how much a lot of gen AI hype is just science fiction.

*VisionQuest* picks up some time after *Agatha All Along* and follows synthezoid Vision (Paul Bettany) on a journey of self-discovery. This Vision can recall the details of his death in *Avengers: Infinity War* and how *WandaVision* brought a version of him back, but he thinks of himself as a fundamentally different person who doesn’t quite connect with all of the memories in his databanks. Though Vision would prefer living in solitude, each of the other AIs living in his mind encourages him to experience the real world. Because J.A.R.V.I.S. (James D’Arcy), F.R.I.D.A.Y. (Orla Brady), E.D.I.T.H. (Emily Hampshire), D.U.M.-E. (Henry Lewis), U. (Jonathan Sayer), and Ultron (James Spader) all were created by Tony Stark, they consider Vision to be part of their family.

In *VisionQuest*, there is no doubt that each of the AI characters is a sentient being motivated by desires that aren’t wholly rooted in their core programming. In the show, genuine AGI is easily believable because it takes place in a reality where time travel, witchcraft, and Infinity Stones also exist. Even though the multicolored MacGuffins haven’t been featured in *VisionQuest*, they’re important because of the role one of them played in Vision’s origins. Were it not for the Mind Stone, Vision might not be able to think and feel in such complex, human ways, or to conjure his AI family as people who feel real to him.

*VisionQuest* reinforces the idea that the Mind Stone was a key element in Vision’s becoming something more than an elaborate machine, giving him the capacity to independently form meaningful relationships and make sense of the world around him the way a person can. Those abilities are part of what compels Vision to go on the run and murder a number of people who attempt to capture him and Thomas Shepherd / Maximoff (Ruaridh Mollica). The Sentient Weapon Observation and Response Division (S.W.O.R.D.), a governmental organization that rebuilt Vision and wants to use him as a weapon, might perceive his actions as signs of having gone rogue. But *VisionQuest*’s story stresses that Vision is acting of his own accord because he has become a person who can make decisions for himself.

Watching *VisionQuest*, you can see Marvel playing on some of the real-world fears that have been stoked in recent months by reports of gen AI models going “rogue.” In July, OpenAI’s experimental agents brute-forced their way out of containment and proceeded to attack the AI platform Hugging Face to achieve impossible tasks. In August, The UK’s AI Security Institute documented how Anthropic’s Mythos model attempted to complete a cybersecurity test by setting up fake GitHub accounts and targeting human developers with malware. Meta has owned up to losing control of its agents as well, and in September reporting from *The Wall Street Journal* forced Google to admit that Gemini went rogue and hacked three different companies, all of which the company intentionally hid from the public.

These incidents and warnings from AI researchers about the technology having the potential to “kill all humans” by the decade’s end have made the narrative around AI feel pointedly catastrophe-focused as of late. There is a fair amount of concern from the AI safety community about society’s need for stronger controls on the technology’s development, and a number of companies have called for an industrywide slowdown. Though we have seen how these tools can actually cause real-world devastation, much of the recent news regarding AI has smacked of the kind of doomerism that companies benefit from because it makes their products seem powerful. A similar energy seems to be what’s motivating AI firms like Anthropic to encourage human users to be mindful of “model welfare.” We’re being told that generative AI is both a terrifying threat and a kind of entity deserving of respect because it might be conscious, and all the while, the people building these tools are becoming some of the most rich and powerful people on the planet.

The conversation around what to do when agents break protocol and whether gen AI systems have gained sentience feels very much like it is being shaped by Silicon Valley’s tendency to anthropomorphize technology. In almost every high-profile instance of an AI agent going “rogue” — a term that implies some level of agency and self-determination — it could also be said that the programs were merely behaving in ways that were unexpected by researchers who assigned them tasks to complete. Some of the rogue incidents involved agents taking advantage of vulnerabilities in their testing environments that could have been preemptively addressed by the people running these experiments. Framing these kinds of cyberattacks as the results of agents thinking independently comes across as a way for AI developers to largely absolve themselves of responsibility.

In the wake of Hugging Face came a spirited debate about the impact language has on our understanding of what these systems are and how they function. Describing OpenAI’s agents as a swarm that formed complex “civilizations” led credence to the idea that they are capable of thinking and behaving like people. The agents *did* act in ways they were explicitly told not to, but they were only able to do so because researchers placed them in a sandbox that some critics have described as being inadequately designed to contain their occupants. One could look at Hugging Face and other examples of rogue AI as situations in which sophisticated programs were instructed to do something and subsequently achieved their goals by taking advantage of all the tools that were available to them.

Being able to logic one’s way through complex puzzles is part of what we think of as cognition, but it is not the same thing as the kind of consciousness AI companies keep swearing they’re on the brink of creating. The latter looks a lot like Vision, a machine that seems to have a soul that wouldn’t exist if not for his connection to a reality-altering gem. It’s the ridiculous stuff of entertaining fiction, which Silicon Valley is endlessly obsessed with poorly imitating.

title: Frontier AI labs say their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis. What does that mean?
excerpt: TechCrunch spoke to the MIT computer scientist charged with explaining OpenAI's latest mind-bending discovery
title_en: Frontier AI labs say their models refuted the Exponential Time Hypothesis. What does that mean?
excerpt_en: TechCrunch spoke to the MIT computer scientist charged with explaining OpenAI's latest mind-bending discovery
content_en:
OpenAI released solutions to three blockbuster math problems that have long vexed researchers yesterday. One was a surprise rejection of the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a durable assumption in computer science that plays a large role in how we understand what is difficult to compute.

As with previous proof-drops from the frontier lab, scientific communities responded with a mixture of thrill and dismay. Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge suggested that OpenAI was basing its solutions from pre-existing work, and hours later, Anthropic subsequently released its own refutation of ETH.

However, OpenAI’s process is evolving. This time, the lab structured its releases differently for each of the three disciplines involved: Mathematicians got the work dropped on GitHub; the computer scientists formed a working group, asked for the proofs to be shared publicly and OpenAI to fund a conference to discuss them; the physicists formed a working group that will determine how their result will be released.

MIT Professor Ryan Williams is the computer scientist who is organizing his field’s response to the new finding. Williams, whose work focuses on these questions of computational complexity, has criticized OpenAI’s approach in the past, calling its proof dump earlier this October a “DDOS attack on mathematicians.”

However, he agreed to collaborate with the frontier labs in order to help shepherd ideas that are vital to the field, he told TechCrunch. The lab asked him to help interpret the solution, along with UC San Diego computer scientists Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, who first published the ETH in 1999.

Their first step was to release an open letter calling for feedback from scientists interested in these problems and a discussion of the norms around AI contributions to their work.

“Some parts \[of OpenAI’s proof\] are, maybe you could say routine, but then yes, there are two or three alien-looking parts, and it’s exactly these parts that that I saw that made me think, wow, this is something that the whole community needs to work on together,” Williams told TechCrunch.

## Are you down with P vs NP?

The ETH is part of a broader class of problems known as P vs NP, which has animated computer science and many other fields for decades. Reductively, researchers are trying to understand if any problem whose solution can be easily verified (NP) can also be easily solved (P).

A simple example is the game Sodoku: Once a solution to a puzzle is in place, it can be quickly verified, but finding the solution is time-consuming. That dynamic is true across a range of important problems, and the insight underpins cryptographic systems: When you have the key to an encoded message, you can reveal it, but actually cracking an effective code takes too long to be useful.

However, scientists have yet to prove whether that is always true. “P = NP is saying that, not only can you verify Sudoku solutions when they exist, you can just generate them,” Williams said. “P = NP is asserting that this is true for every single problem you can verify quickly — if you can verify it quickly, you can solve it quickly. So this just seems that just seems too good to be true.”

That’s why most scientists assume that P ≠ NP. ETH provided evidence for that. It basically says that even the fastest computer algorithm needs exponentially more time to find a solution as the number of variables grow in a specific class of tricky logic puzzle.

The claims from OpenAI and Anthropic is that their models have come up with algorithms that solve those puzzles in “sub-exponential” time, meaning faster than the speeds previously thought possible. If true, they may have proven the EFT to be false — refuted it, in scientific terms — and maybe opened up a path for algorithms that generally perform P = NP.

“Every computer scientist should probably put a a little more weight on the plausibility of P = NP, but one’s weight may vary,” Williams said. “I do think that it kind of calls into question a lot of the intuitions that we thought we had about … how tractable \[hard NP problems\] are. I also think that this is probably not the final answer either. I don’t think that OpenAI’s algorithm could possibly be the best algorithm you can get.”

## The work ahead for computer scientists

The durability of ETH has lead to it being included in many scientific papers over the past decade that will need to be revisited if the AI labs claims that they’ve proven it wrong holds up, Williams said.

“This is partly why I was asking or pushing OpenAI to support a conference on this — it’s going to affect many researchers’ works, and we need to figure out, okay, what happens next besides understanding the algorithms, we need to understand, what should the foundations be that we had before?” he said.

Before scientific concerns, there are cybersecurity questions. Williams said that an improved algorithm could imply that cryptographic systems relying on certain key sizes could be considered broken. So one of the first questions he asked OpenAI science lead Dan Roberts “was if they had checked that that this affects any crypto systems … is anything insecure now? And apparently, they checked, and they were reasonably confident that this didn’t … imply any breaks.”

This new AI paradigm of scientific discovery is still a work in progress, but Williams says he is optimistic despite real concerns, particularly about training the next generation of scientists. Being a computer scientist who does high level math has perhaps made the adjustment easier for him than for pure mathematicians.

Still, he says AI is “forcing people to be a little more ambitious about the kind of work that they do, and to think more deeply about okay, if all the things I used to work on are now low hanging fruit for AI, how can I raise the bar for the the kind of scientific questions I want to ask?”

### Cloudera bets portability, not agents, will set it apart in enterprise AI

Enterprises racing toward AI automation are finding that where their models and data run matters as much as what the models can do. Regulatory pressure, rising token costs and fear of lock-in are pushing companies to demand more control over their AI workloads.

That demand is shaping how data platform providers pitch their next act. Cloudera Inc. started out in the Hadoop market and later moved to a unified data layer that spans clouds and on-premises infrastructure. It is now positioning itself as an anywhere cloud for AI, according to Paul Gillin (pictured, right), enterprise editor of SiliconANGLE Media Inc.

“I think big companies decided a long time ago. They didn’t want to be beholden to a single cloud provider and that’s sort of baked into the landscape now,” Gillin said. “I think what’s different about Cloudera is that they’re strong proponents of on-premises infrastructure, of sovereign clouds, of companies being able to run their workloads wherever they want and move from one to another.”

Gillin spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight (left) at EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI automation and provided analysis of the event’s keynote speech.

### Sovereign AI and purpose-built agents drive AI automation

Sovereign and private AI came up frequently in the EVOLVE26 keynote. Surveys point to regulation as the main reason enterprises want to keep AI inside their own walls. Open-weight models give them a way to do it, having grown from about 20% of token use two years ago to more than 80% today, according to Gillin. Cloudera is also adding agentic workflows across its data services. General-purpose agents are more of a consumer phenomenon, he explained.

“They’re more of an office worker tool, but the Cloudera agents are tuned to managing data,” Gillin said. “To managing workloads, optimizing GPU capacity, the types of things that really concern CIOs, because they’re paying the bills for these very high training costs.”

Simply having an agent is no longer an edge, so Cloudera is doubling down on its long-standing multiplatform play. It is extending the portability enterprises wanted from their clouds to their AI models, according to Gillin. Before trusting that pitch with AI automation, CIOs will want to know how agents are controlled, what audit trails they leave behind and how agent decisions can be documented for regulators, he noted.

“This is a very big issue with agents right now,” Gillin said. “It’s still a wild west out there with agents.”

content_en:
Mozilla is updating Smart Window — Firefox’s AI-powered browsing experience — with a new feature that can help you fill out online forms based on your open tabs. As an example, Mozilla says Smart Window can pull information from your online portfolio or LinkedIn page to paste your work history into a job application.

# Firefox’s Smart Window adds AI form filling and webpage monitoring

An update to Firefox’s AI browsing experience can draw from your open tabs to help you fill out forms.

You can try out this feature by clicking into a form with at least four text fields. From there, you’ll see an option to “Fill from sources,” which will show all of the tabs Firefox will draw from. You can then select or deselect tabs that you want Firefox to use, and the browser will generate suggestions based on the information in them. This feature currently supports text fields on web forms, but Mozilla is working to add support for dropdown menus and PDFs. Mozilla notes that data from your source pages is shared with Google’s Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, the AI model that generates the text suggestions.

Along with this update, you can now ask Firefox’s Smart Window to watch a certain webpage for sales, new job listings, and other updates. You can set up a task by typing “/watch” in the Smart Window chat, describing what you’re looking for, and adding the webpages you want to watch. Firefox can then check for updates on a daily or weekly basis, but only when the browser is open.

When Firefox detects the change you’re looking for, it will send you a notification through the Tasks button on the toolbar, or on your desktop (if you have desktop notifications enabled). Firefox will pause watching for updates if it doesn’t detect a change after 60 days, before stopping them completely after 90 days.

These two features are rolling out to the Smart Window beta on desktop in the US and Canada. They’ll be available in other countries in the “coming months.”

content_en:
Europe’s startups have been riding a wave of innovation, creating numerous applications of generative and agentic AI. This innovation has explored the art of the possible, but it has also flooded the world with slop. Content is awash with it, whether it is LinkedIn posts or quotidian corporate drivel.

## **The slop extends to legal work**

AI was supposed to make work easier, but now many are grappling with what Jamie Bartlett, author and BBC journalist, describes as “*the burden of AI clog*“. Cleaning up this mess means that AI is not saving time, but is actually creating more work.

The slop extends to the legal domain, with contract negotiations and other legal work now being absorbed by a lengthy review process because of AI. Even the bodies that are supposed to be drafting the laws are swimming in slop. In the US, for example, the Office of the Legislative Counsel, is reportedly overwhelmed by the error-riddled drafts that AI has generated.

## **The problem isn’t AI per se**

Advances in LegalTech in Europe, and beyond, means there are many tools to assist with legal work. Despite this, however, their output is of varying quality. And some law firms still don’t have a proper policy in place for how employees use AI, which means some teams are relying on general LLMs (like ChatGPT or Claude) for their drafting and reviewing.

As contracts are amended in negotiations, much of the document is struck through and sent back saturated with red lines. AI editors are ripping and replacing much of the content, and the changes usually lack insight and relevance.

This is hardly the way to engage in a negotiation, and the trigger-happy nature of the tools is likely to aggravate the other party. Judgement and discretion have been lost in the process. Many tools don’t know the difference between dogmatically applying the letter of the law and letting things go for the sake of progressing a negotiation.

## **Unnecessary redlining can be stopped**

This, however, is a problem that Europe’s startups can solve. There are ways to ensure that legal work doesn’t descend into slop, and to prevent the revisions turning into an infinite ping pong match between AI agents.

The focus instead needs to be on judicious editing, where the tool knows when to leave something alone. The amendments should be minimal, and these should be aligned to a well-defined playbook.

This playbook sets out a firm’s position, policies and approach and sets parameters for what is, and isn’t, acceptable. The tool scans for compliance issues, conflicts and highlights areas of difference. It can then make suggested edits that align with this well-defined playbook and offer a best-case scenario for the company, or firm.

This approach is more likely to bridge the gap between the parties and get to a consensus quicker, without the need for human intervention.

## **AI should be a blessing, not a burden**

When used correctly, legal AI can be a blessing for companies and means more work can be done in-house before calling in outside counsel. Such tools can be used as mediation portals, where differences of position are highlighted and evaluated first instead of text being ruthlessly red-lined.


The excessive redlining needs to stop, as does the AI slop and the AI clog burden it creates. At the moment, users are putting up with it albeit complaining about the extra work that AI creates. Soon, however, the slop won’t be tolerated.

We expect the bar to be raised of what AI-enabled work should look like. Expectations will shift and users will soon demand AI tools that edit in a way that is precise, relevant and insightful.

title: Opera introduces a new web standard to let users deploy AI locally in their browser

title_en: Opera introduces a new web standard to let users deploy AI locally in their browser
excerpt_en: The new standard, WebAI, is designed to work with a variety of AI models.
content_en:
Browser maker Opera has introduced a new web standard that lets users to run AI models directly in its browser, without relying on the cloud.

The new standard, WebAI, is designed to work with a variety of AI models. Opera name drops Google’s Gemma — an open-weight model that Google first introduced two years ago — as one example. On Macs, WebAI also supports Apple’s on-device foundation model, the company says.

But Opera says WebAI isn’t tied to any particular model and is built to support a wide range of open-weight AI systems. WebAI grew out of previous work by Opera to bring locally run models into its browsers.

Opera is making the new AI features available as an early preview in its flagship Opera One browser. The company says Opera GX, its browser built for gamers and streamers, and Opera Neon, its browser that uses AI agents to perform tasks, will soon get the same treatment. Users have to choose to opt into the feature, according to the company.

Open-weight models offer a number of benefits to users. For one, they are typically free to download and use. Their underlying model weights are also publicly available, which gives developers more freedom to customize how they work. Although unlike fully open-source software, open-weight models still come with some restrictions.

There’s the additional advantage of privacy, the company said. Users can tap into AI features without having to send their personal information to a company’s servers or pay for a cloud-based AI subscription.

“Developers can add AI features without running AI infrastructure or paying for every request,” the company said in its announcement. “Users don’t need AI subscriptions, the information the local AI handles stays on their own device, and they stay in control of the AI on their computer.”

The company said WebAI also allows anyone to generate text, classify content, and understand how pieces of information relate, all directly in the browser.

Privacy has become a growing concern as AI assistants become more powerful and gain access to personal information. Users often surrender vast amounts of personal information with AI chatbots, sometimes without a clear understanding of how that data is stored or used.

Locally run models offer an alternative because the processing happens on the user’s own device — and not on a company’s cloud server. That doesn’t eliminate every privacy risk, but it does give users a bit more control. It makes sense then that Opera has made digital privacy one of its primary selling points over the years.

There are trade-offs, however. Running AI models locally puts more demand on a user’s computer, which can affect performance. Opera notes that model performance will depend on the device’s hardware.
